name: OpenTofu
summary: The open-source fork of Terraform, created after HashiCorp’s 2023 licence change: same HCL, same providers, `tofu` instead of `terraform`.
intro: OpenTofu works the way Terraform does. You declare resources in HCL files, `tofu plan` compares them with a state file and shows what will be created, changed or destroyed, and `tofu apply` calls the cloud APIs through provider plugins. It began as a copy of Terraform’s last MPL-licensed code, so existing configurations, modules and providers work unchanged, and the project calls it a drop-in replacement: it reads state files created by Terraform up to the 1.5.x versions. Providers and modules come from the OpenTofu Registry, a public index kept in a git repository, where publishing is a pull request.

Since the fork the two tools have moved apart. OpenTofu added features the community had asked HashiCorp for: client-side encryption of state and plan files (1.7, April 2024), variables in backend and module source settings (1.8), and `for_each` on provider blocks for multi-region setups (1.9). Code that uses OpenTofu-only features can live in `.tofu` files, which OpenTofu reads in preference to a `.tf` file of the same name, so one module can serve both tools. The project started at the Linux Foundation in September 2023 and was accepted into the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a Sandbox project in April 2025. Version 1.13, released at the end of September 2026, is supported until August 2027.
strengths: Open source under MPL 2.0 with neutral foundation governance, so it can be embedded in commercial products and hosted services that Terraform’s BSL rules out
Familiar to anyone who knows Terraform: the same HCL, the same providers and a documented migration path
Built-in state and plan encryption with a passphrase or a key from AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault or OpenBao, whatever backend stores the state
Features Terraform doesn’t have, such as `for_each` over providers and variables in backend configuration
limits: The two tools keep diverging: OpenTofu-only syntax won’t run on Terraform, and migration is documented for state from Terraform 1.5.x and earlier
The same model’s chores as Terraform: a state file to store, lock and protect, and drift whenever someone edits resources by hand
Encrypted state is unrecoverable without its key; the docs tell you to back up keys and an unencrypted state copy before turning it on
Still a CNCF Sandbox project, the earliest maturity level, which the CNCF describes as experimental

story: Terraform was open source under the Mozilla Public License from its release in 2014, and a large ecosystem of modules, providers and companies grew around it. On August 10, 2023, HashiCorp moved it to the Business Source License, which allows free use but forbids competing with HashiCorp’s own products. Companies whose products were built on Terraform published the OpenTF Manifesto (now the OpenTofu Manifesto), calling the new licence vague and a “poison pill” and asking HashiCorp to return Terraform to open source. Gruntwork, Spacelift, Harness, env0 and Scalr were among those behind it.

HashiCorp didn’t, so they forked the last MPL code. On September 20, 2023, the Linux Foundation announced the project under its new name, OpenTofu, with pledges from more than 140 organisations and 600 individuals. The first stable release, 1.6.0, came out on January 10, 2024 after four months of work by almost 60 contributors, with a new registry and a testing feature.

The project then shipped what the community had long wanted from Terraform. State encryption in 1.7, released in April 2024, came from an RFC by a community member who had tried for years to get it into Terraform. In April 2025 OpenTofu was accepted into the CNCF Sandbox, and it has shipped a new minor version every few months since, reaching 1.13 in September 2026.

choices.choice: Fork from the last open-source release
choices.why: Starting from Terraform’s MPL code kept every existing configuration, module and provider working, so switching could be as simple as installing a different binary.

choices.choice: Stay backward compatible, and mark the differences
choices.why: Users had years of Terraform code. New features land in OpenTofu, and the `.tofu` file extension lets module authors use them while keeping `.tf` files for Terraform users.
The fork existed because one company could change the licence. Placing it under the Linux Foundation, and later the CNCF, means no single vendor can relicense it.

choices.choice: A registry that is just a git repository
choices.why: The team consulted the authors of earlier registries such as Homebrew’s and built a Homebrew-like index, so publishing a provider or module is a pull request.
